title: Prediction of One Repetition Maximum Strength From Multiple Repetition Maximum Testing and Anthropometry
authors: Reynolds JM, Gordon TJ, Robergs RA
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 70 adults (34 men, 36 women) aged 18-69 years who completed 1, 5, 10 and 20 repetition maximum tests on the flat barbell bench press (chest press) and the plate-loaded leg press
findings: The decrease in the load lifted from 1 to 5, 10 and 20 repetitions to failure was nonlinear for both lifts; the nonlinear fit was much closer than a linear one (leg press standard error 2.6 kg nonlinear against 11.0 kg linear; chest press 0.2 kg against 2.6 kg).

The 5RM data gave the best prediction of 1RM: R2 for the 5, 10 and 20RM conditions was 0.974, 0.933 and 0.915 for the leg press and 0.993, 0.976 and 0.955 for the chest press. The leg press equation from 5RM was 1RM = 1.0970 x 5RM weight (kg) + 14.2546, with a standard error of 16.16 kg.
The authors conclude that 1RM can be accurately estimated from multiple repetition testing, and that no more than 10 repetitions should be used in linear equations for the leg press and chest press.
limitations: Two machine or bench lifts (not a free-weight squat or a hinge), 70 volunteers of mixed ages, repetitions taken to failure; the equations are for the lifts tested. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: Any estimate of a maximum from a few repetitions is an approximation, best from low repetitions: a linear equation should stay at 10 repetitions or fewer. The engine's block sets (3-6 repetitions plus 1-3 in reserve) stay inside that; a ramp-in set of 8 repetitions with 3 in reserve reaches 11, one above it. A set above 10 repetitions to the limit (done plus left) therefore gives no estimate (`f8.e1rmMaxReps`, a default taken from this advice, grade D). The estimate is shown as an estimate and is never a test (grade D).
Gives no check of the engine's divisor (f8.e1rmDivisor); the corpus holds no paper that validates it.

r2.note: Three named authors; Europe PMC holds the first author's affiliation (Exercise Physiology Laboratories, Exercise Science Program, University of New Mexico). No separate university record was fetched. No interest is stated in the abstract.

r3.note: Published 2006, not corrected. nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm (7289 people, 269 studies) supersedes it for the repetitions at a percentage of 1RM; its advice to use a linear equation to no more than 10 repetitions is not contradicted, and richens-2014-reps-at-percent-runners shows runners reaching 20-40 repetitions at 80-70% of 1RM.

r4.note: The advice of 10 repetitions is this one study's. nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm, lesuer-1997-1rm-equations and richens-2014-reps-at-percent-runners agree that the repetition and load relation is not linear and that equations are biased, but none states a limit. Held.

r5.note: Population stated: 70 adults aged 18-69, flat bench press and plate-loaded leg press. Use for the squat, hinge and calf lifts and for runners is extrapolated.

r6.note: A journal paper keeps the level of its design (a cross-sectional study, level C); the caps by class are for sources outside the journals.
